answer:
**K controls how local the prediction is.** With K=1, one nearby example determines the answer. This can follow a complex boundary but is sensitive to noise or one mislabeled point. With a larger neighborhood, individual accidents average out, while small local patterns may be blurred. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

Imagine a narrow island of positive examples inside a mostly negative region. A small K can preserve that island. A very large K may include so many surrounding negatives that the island disappears from predictions.

At K=N, every query uses the entire training set. Regression returns the same global mean; ordinary classification returns the global majority decision. Variance from local sample fluctuations is low, but bias can be enormous if the target varies with x.

These are broad trends rather than strict monotonic guarantees on every finite dataset. Distance weighting, feature scaling, and density affect the result. Tune K with an appropriate split and inspect rare classes or sparse regions, not just aggregate accuracy. A stable predictor is useful only if it retains the structure the task needs.

**Technical details and references.**

At $K=1$, kNN is highly local and sensitive to individual samples: usually low bias and high variance. Increasing $K$ smooths predictions, generally increasing bias and reducing variance. At $K=N$, every query receives the global training mean or class-frequency decision. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

These are trends, not strict monotonic guarantees for every dataset or metric. Distance scaling, class imbalance, sample density, and distance weighting affect behavior. Choose $K$ with appropriate cross-validation and evaluate rare-class/local-region performance; a globally stable predictor can ignore the structure that matters for the task.
